title: A Portrait for the Hymn
premise: Xanthe Kavanagh, a property surveyor estranged from her family, is hired to appraise her late grandmother's house and discovers the appraisal itself is an instrument: every measurement she takes feeds a founding ritual that has kept the house alive on borrowed identities for two centuries. The extra chair in the photographs is the seat reserved for the next resident, and the house intends it to be hers. To escape, Xanthe must complete the interrupted ritual by signing the papers in her grandmother's name rather than her own, transferring the debt backward to the dead instead of forward to herself. In the final chapter she signs, burns the portrait of the first founder, and walks out as the house collapses into ordinary rot — though one photograph, taken afterward, still shows the chair, now empty, waiting.
about_author: Xanthe Brightwater is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent years cataloguing structural anomalies in inherited properties across coastal New England. Their fiction draws on real survey reports, family probate disputes, and the uncanny habit of old houses to remember their owners.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. Arriving to appraise her grandmother's house, Xanthe finds decades of family photographs in which an empty wooden chair appears beside each subject — including photos taken before the chair existed. Her measurements keep returning impossible numbers: rooms larger inside than out. The emotional beat is uneasy denial; she catalogs rational explanations for everything, but the chapter ends with her laser measure reading a distance to a person standing behind her. No one is there.

chapters.title: Provenance
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe, with interpolated pages from the founders' 1820s ledger. Researching the deed, Xanthe learns the house was built by four signatories who bound their names into its foundations, each generation's resident renewing the contract by appraising and 'accepting' the property. Her grandmother died mid-renewal, leaving the ritual incomplete and the house starving. The beat is dread deepening into complicity: Xanthe realizes her professional measurements have already been feeding it, and the chair in the photos now sits closer to the camera in every picture she takes.

chapters.title: The Sitting
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. The house stops pretending. Rooms rearrange to trap her, the walls sweat sap, and the founders' portraits begin repainting themselves with her face layered under theirs. She discovers the previous residents didn't die — they were absorbed, their identities worn like coats by the house. The climax builds as she finds her own completed portrait hanging where her grandmother's was, signed in her handwriting. The beat is terror curdling into fury: she refuses to be furniture, and tears the portrait down, breaking the house's patience.

chapters.title: Countersign
chapters.summary: POV: Xanthe. Hunted through a house that is now mostly throat, Xanthe reaches the closing table and understands the loophole: the ritual requires a signature, not a specific signer. She signs the renewal papers in her dead grandmother's name, invoking a hand the house cannot refuse but cannot hold, then burns the founder's original portrait to sever the chain. The house folds inward, aging centuries in minutes. The resolution is bittersweet survival: Xanthe inherits nothing but her own name, and one last photograph shows the chair — empty, patient, and no longer hers.
